summary: Teach a/b as a copies of the unit fraction 1/b, where 1/b is the definite amount made by ONE part when a whole is cut into b EQUAL parts. Build the unit fraction first as a quantity, then iterate it (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4). The pivotal insight is that the denominator names how many equal parts the whole is split into — and so, for a given whole, fixes the SIZE of each part — while the numerator counts how many such parts are taken. Within any comparison keep the whole fixed and insist parts be equal (equal area in area models, equal length on lengths/number lines, equal number in sets); vary b on a fixed whole so part-size visibly depends on the denominator, and vary the kind of whole across separate tasks so the idea is not tied to one picture.
misconceptions: Equal-parts ignored — any b pieces are called bths regardless of size (IES Roadblock 1.2)
Counting shaded parts mechanically without grasping that numerator and denominator together name one quantity (IES caution)
Reading the denominator as a group SIZE ('thirds = groups of three') rather than the number of equal parts
Whole-number bias — a bigger denominator means a bigger part or a bigger value
Non-unit fraction taken as a unit fraction — for 3/4 shading just one part

activities.title: Cut it fair, then count the unit
steps: Take one whole bar (a chocolate bar works well) and cut it into equal parts, e.g. 6, checking that the parts are genuinely equal in area before accepting them.
Shade ONE part and name it as a quantity: 'this is one-sixth, 1/6'.
Build 2/6, then 3/6, by copying that single 1/6 piece and counting as you go, saying 'two one-sixths, three one-sixths' and writing the label each time.
Reset the sixths bar to show 2/6, then set an identical bar beside it, cut into 4 equal parts, and shade 2 parts on it (so you have 2/6 next to 2/4).
Slide the two shaded regions over one another to compare how much chocolate each shows, and state which is more and why.
activities.insight: a/b is a copies of an equal part whose size is fixed by the denominator; shading the same NUMBER of parts does not give the same amount, because sixths are smaller than fourths of the same whole (so 2/6 < 2/4).

activities.title: How big is ONE part? (vary the whole and the denominator)
steps: Build the SAME fraction across different wholes — a bar, a circle, a fraction strip, a length/number line, a set of objects (e.g. 2 of every 6), and Cuisenaire rods with one chosen rod as the whole.
On a number line, make the fraction by repeating a jump of size 1/b, a times, instead of shading an area.
Re-cut one bar into 8 equal parts and name one part (1/8); compare its size to one quarter of that same bar and state which is bigger and why.
Draw a given fraction, e.g. 2/6, of the SAME whole a DIFFERENT way — differently shaped parts but the same amount.
For each model, answer not just 'how many are shaded?' but 'how big is ONE part?'
activities.insight: The same fraction names the same relationship to its whole (and the same number) whatever picture is used, but the amount it shows depends on the size of the whole; for any given whole the denominator controls how many equal parts it is cut into (regardless of that whole's shape), and more equal parts of the SAME whole means each part is smaller (1/8 < 1/4).

activities.title: Predict, then check: comparing same-numerator fractions
steps: Before cutting, look at two identical bars. Predict and give a REASON: if 2 parts are shaded on a bar cut into 4, and 2 parts on an identical bar cut into 6, which shows more chocolate — or the same? State the reason out loud BEFORE observing.
Then cut both bars and slide the shaded regions over each other to check.
Revise or confirm your prediction, explaining what the comparison showed.
Build 3/4 from single pieces and say how many quarters and how big each one is.
Tackle the trap question: could 3/4 of a small bar be LESS chocolate than 1/2 of a big bar? State what must be true about the wholes to compare the amounts fairly.
activities.insight: With the whole held fixed, more equal parts means each part is smaller, so 2/4 > 2/6 and 3/4 > 3/6 even though the counts match; comparing the AMOUNTS shown by two models is only fair when the wholes are the same size, though the fractions themselves, as numbers, remain comparable (3/4 > 1/2 always).

activities.title: Identify, match and construct across models (consolidation)
steps: Identify the fraction shaded in a given model, e.g. one shaded part of a shape in 5 equal parts named as 1/5.
Match a written fraction a/b to the model that shows it.
Sort models into 'equal parts' vs 'not equal parts', and judge whether a bar cut into 4 UNEQUAL pieces with one shaded really shows a quarter.
Construct a requested fraction yourself — draw it, or choose/colour the right number of equal parts.
Explain in words what the denominator and numerator each tell you for one chosen example.
activities.insight: Secure, flexible recognition and construction of a/b across representations, with equal parts as the non-negotiable criterion.

checkQuestion: Show a bar cut into 4 equal parts with 3 shaded. Ask: 'What fraction is shaded? In your own words, what does the 4 tell us and what does the 3 tell us?' Then show an identical bar cut into 6 equal parts with 3 shaded and ask: 'Is this more chocolate, less, or the same as the first — and why?'
checkAnswer: 3/4. The 4 (denominator) tells how many EQUAL parts the whole is cut into, so each part is 1/4; the 3 (numerator) counts how many of those parts we take, i.e. 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The second bar shows 3/6, which is LESS than 3/4: both have 3 shaded parts, but each sixth is smaller than each fourth because the same whole is cut into more pieces.
